It's a bit further and genuinely best attempted only on a forecast-confirmed clear day, but for Fuji-focused travelers it delivers the picture-perfect shot Hakone can only promise on luck. Hakone is the easier all-rounder; Kawaguchiko is the Fuji specialist.

Which day trip to pick

  • Mountains, hot springs, and Fuji in one: Hakone.
  • Grand historic shrines and forest: Nikko.
  • Easy, scenic, temples-plus-sea: Kamakura.
  • The clearest, closest Mt Fuji views: the Fuji Five Lakes / Kawaguchiko.

All are reachable by train, and depending on your route a Japan Rail Pass or a regional pass can make the fares more economical — though for a single day trip, individual tickets are often cheaper, so do the math.

Practical tips

  • Start early to make the most of the day, since travel each way eats into your time.
  • Check the weather, especially for anything Fuji-related — the mountain hides behind clouds often, so a clear forecast dramatically improves the trip.
  • Consider a regional transport pass for places like Hakone, which bundle the area's railways, ropeway, and boat.
  • Guided tours exist for all of these if you'd rather not navigate the connections yourself, and can be worth booking ahead in peak season.
  • Bring layers — the mountains (Hakone, Nikko, Fuji) are cooler than central Tokyo.

How many day trips is too many

Fitting two or three of these into a single Tokyo stay is tempting, and one or even two is genuinely reasonable — but each day trip costs a full day of your limited Tokyo time, not just the hours spent traveling. Three day trips out of a five-day Tokyo-plus-Kyoto trip means barely two days actually spent in the city itself, which usually isn't the balance most first-timers actually want once they're standing in Shibuya wishing they had more time there. Pick the one or two that genuinely matter to you, and let the rest wait for a return trip — weighing day trips against city time is one piece of the larger route-planning puzzle that the complete Japan route guide works through in full.

Bottom line

Tokyo's day trips add real variety to a trip — hot springs, ornate shrines, a seaside Buddha, and Japan's most famous mountain, all an easy train ride away. Pick based on your interests and the weather, start early, and any of them turns into a memorable break from the big city.

title: Hakone Day Trip Guide: Hot Springs and Mt Fuji Views
excerpt: Hakone is the classic mountain escape from Tokyo — onsen, Mt Fuji views, and a scenic loop of railways and boats. Here's how to do it.
content:
Hakone is the go-to mountain and hot-spring escape from Tokyo, famous for its onsen, dramatic volcanic scenery, and — on clear days — postcard views of Mt Fuji. It's close enough for a day trip, though an overnight in a ryokan makes it even better. Part of its charm is that getting around is an experience in itself: a loop of scenic mountain transport that strings the sights together. Here's how to do it.

What makes Hakone special

Hakone combines several attractions into one compact, scenic area: natural hot springs (onsen), steaming volcanic valleys, a beautiful lake, world-class art museums, and Mt Fuji views. It's long been a favorite weekend retreat for Tokyoites, and for visitors it delivers a concentrated dose of mountain Japan within easy reach of the capital.

The classic Hakone loop

A typical day strings together a series of charming transport modes — itself the highlight for many:

  • Hakone Tozan mountain railway that switchbacks up the forested hillside.
  • Hakone Ropeway (cable car) gliding over Owakudani, a steaming, sulphurous volcanic valley where you can try the famous black eggs (kuro-tamago) cooked in the hot springs — said to add years to your life.
  • Sightseeing boat (often pirate-ship themed) across scenic Lake Ashi, with Mt Fuji views on clear days.
  • Buses and a cable car connecting the pieces into a full loop.

The Hakone Free Pass covers this transport for a set number of days and saves both money and hassle if you're doing the full circuit.

Getting there

The most comfortable way in is the Odakyu Romancecar, a reserved-seat limited express running direct from Tokyo's Shinjuku Station to Hakone-Yumoto (the loop's starting point) in about 85 minutes — worth booking the seat in advance on busy weekends. It's a separate ticket from the Hakone Free Pass, though combined tickets bundling both are commonly sold at Shinjuku's Odakyu ticket counters and are usually the best value if you're doing the full loop.

Highlights to add

  • Soak in an onsen — the whole point of Hakone for many; numerous ryokan and day-use bathhouses are available, some with Fuji or valley views.
  • Hakone Open-Air Museum — a celebrated sculpture park blending modern art with mountain scenery, with a notable Picasso collection.
  • Hakone Shrine — with its iconic red torii gate standing in the waters of Lake Ashi, one of the area's most photographed spots.
  • Owakudani — the dramatic volcanic valley, its black eggs, and views.

Day trip or overnight?

Hakone is doable as a day trip from Tokyo, especially if you focus on the scenic loop and a day-use onsen. But to truly relax — and to maximize your Fuji-viewing chances across both evening and morning — an overnight ryokan stay is wonderful, with a kaiseki dinner and a soak under the stars. If your schedule allows, one night in a Hakone onsen ryokan is a trip highlight in itself.

Tips for clear Fuji views

Mt Fuji is famously shy, often hidden by cloud. To improve your odds, check the weather forecast and aim for a clear day; mornings and the colder, clearer months (late autumn through winter) tend to offer the best visibility. Don't count on the view — but when it appears across Lake Ashi, it's unforgettable. Hakone is also just one of several places on a Tokyo-based trip that promise a Fuji glimpse (the Shinkansen and some Tokyo skyscraper observation decks are others on a clear day), so if it clouds over here, you're not necessarily out of chances — deciding how much of your itinerary to build around chasing the mountain is exactly the kind of trade-off the complete Japan route guide weighs in.

Practical notes

  • Start early to fit the full loop into a day — it takes several hours to complete.
  • Consider the Hakone Free Pass for the railways, ropeway, cable car, and boat.
  • Bring layers — it's noticeably cooler in the mountains than in Tokyo.
  • Occasionally the ropeway over Owakudani closes due to volcanic activity; check on the day, as there are bus alternatives.
  • Guided tours exist if you'd rather not navigate the connections yourself.
  • Try more than the eggs — Hakone-Yumoto's main street has plenty of soba noodle shops and yosegi-zaiku (marquetry woodwork) souvenir stores worth a browse while you wait for a train or bus connection — yosegi-zaiku dates to the Edo period and uses only the natural colors of different woods, no paint or stain, to build its intricate geometric patterns.

Bottom line

Hakone packs hot springs, volcanic drama, lake scenery, art, and Mt Fuji into one scenic loop within easy reach of Tokyo. Do it as a full day or, ideally, an overnight ryokan stay — and hope for clear skies to catch Fuji across the lake, though even a cloudy day here is still a genuinely good day out.

title: Himeji Castle Day Trip Guide
excerpt: Himeji Castle is Japan's finest original castle, an easy Shinkansen trip from Kyoto or Osaka. Here's what to see and how to plan your visit.
content:
Himeji Castle is widely regarded as Japan's most spectacular castle — a brilliant white hilltop fortress nicknamed the "White Heron" for its elegant, soaring form. Crucially, unlike many Japanese castles that are 20th-century concrete reconstructions, Himeji is an original, surviving structure and a UNESCO World Heritage site. It makes a rewarding day trip from Kyoto or Osaka, and for anyone interested in history and architecture, it's a standout. Here's how to visit.

Why Himeji is special

Most castles you'll encounter in Japan are postwar rebuilds in concrete, faithful on the outside but modern within. Himeji is the real thing — a genuinely old wooden castle, completed in its current form in the early 1600s, that survived wars, earthquakes, and centuries of time remarkably intact. Its gleaming white plaster walls, layered roofs, and graceful silhouette make it the finest surviving example of Japanese castle architecture. A major restoration completed in 2015 left the exterior dazzlingly white. For history and architecture lovers, it's reason enough for the trip.

What to see

  • The main keep: you climb up through its wooden interior floors — steep stairs, weapon racks, defensive features — to the top, which offers views over the city. The interior is bare wood, giving a real sense of the original structure.
  • The defensive layout: the maze-like approach paths, multiple gates, and angled walls were ingeniously designed to confuse and slow attackers; walking the winding route to the keep is part of the experience.
  • Koko-en Garden: a beautiful Edo-style Japanese garden adjacent to the castle, often combined with a discounted joint ticket — a serene complement to the fortress.
  • The grounds: spectacular in cherry blossom season, when the white castle is framed by clouds of pink.
  • Himeji City Museum of Art and the Hyogo Prefectural Museum of History: a short walk from the castle, both are worth a stop if you want more context on the castle's history without the crowds.

A bit of history

The castle in its current form dates to 1609, built by Ikeda Terumasa after he took control of the domain — though a fortification has stood on the hill since the 14th century, expanded and rebuilt by successive lords. It was never destroyed in battle, survived Allied bombing raids in WWII that flattened much of the surrounding city (a bomb reportedly hit the keep but failed to detonate), and escaped the demolition and "modernization" that claimed many other castles during Japan's rapid postwar development — which is exactly why it's one of the only genuinely original castle keeps left standing in the country.

How to get there

Himeji is farther than the closer Kansai day trips — about 45-55 minutes from Kyoto and 30-45 minutes from Shin-Osaka by Shinkansen — but the Shinkansen makes it very manageable, and the castle is a straightforward walk (about 15–20 minutes) straight down the main avenue from the station, visible ahead of you the whole way. A Japan Rail Pass or a regional Kansai pass can make the fares more economical if you hold one; otherwise buy a ticket. Note that the standard JR Pass doesn't cover the fastest Nozomi service without a supplement, but the covered Hikari and Sakura trains reach Himeji fine. Whether a farther-out trip like this earns a spot on your itinerary, versus staying closer to your base city, is a real trade-off worth thinking through in advance — the complete Japan route guide covers how to weigh it.

How long to spend

Himeji works as a half-day to full-day trip. The castle itself takes a couple of hours to explore properly — more if it's busy, since climbing the keep can involve queues and timed entry at peak periods — plus time for Koko-en Garden. With a full day, you can combine it with a stop in Kobe or Osaka on the way back.

Practical tips

  • Arrive early, especially in cherry blossom season, as the keep can get crowded and entry is sometimes capped at busy times.
  • Wear socks and easy-off shoes — you remove your shoes to climb the wooden keep and carry them in a provided bag.
  • The interior stairs are steep and narrow; wear comfortable clothing and watch your head on low beams.
  • Combine your ticket with Koko-en Garden next door for the discounted rate.
  • Cherry blossom season is stunning but very busy — plan around it accordingly.

Bottom line

For Japan's grandest and most authentic castle, Himeji is well worth the Shinkansen ride. Its dazzling white form, fascinating defensive design, original construction, and UNESCO status make it a standout day trip from Kyoto or Osaka for anyone drawn to history and architecture — the finest castle experience in the country — and given how many "castles" across Japan are 20th-century concrete rebuilds, this may be the only chance on your trip to stand inside one that's genuinely centuries old.

title: Kamakura Day Trip Guide: The Great Buddha by the Sea
excerpt: Kamakura is an easy, relaxed coastal day trip from Tokyo, famous for its open-air Great Buddha, temples, and beaches. Here's how to visit.
content:
Kamakura is a relaxed coastal town within easy reach of Tokyo, best known for its monumental open-air Great Buddha, along with atmospheric temples, shrines, and a breezy seaside setting. Once the political capital of Japan in the medieval era, it's now a laid-back escape that pairs history with sea air — the most relaxing of the classic Tokyo day trips. Here's how to do it.

The Great Buddha (Daibutsu)

Kamakura's signature sight is the Great Buddha, a massive bronze statue over 11 meters tall, seated serenely in the open air at Kotoku-in temple. It was once housed in a great hall, but the building was washed away by a tsunami centuries ago, and the Buddha has sat out in the open ever since — which only adds to its presence and serenity. Standing before it is quietly awe-inspiring, and you can even step inside the hollow statue for a small fee. It's the centerpiece of any Kamakura visit.

Temples and shrines

Kamakura is dotted with historic temples and shrines from its days as the seat of power:

  • Hase-dera: a beautiful temple near the Great Buddha, with gardens, sea views, a revered eleven-headed Kannon statue, and a cave shrine.
  • Tsurugaoka Hachimangu: the town's grand central shrine, approached via a long ceremonial avenue lined with torii gates.
  • Hokokuji (the Bamboo Temple): a serene temple with a lovely bamboo grove and a tea house, quieter than Kyoto's famous version.
  • Numerous smaller temples scattered through the wooded hills, some along pleasant hiking trails.
  • Meigetsu-in: a temple famous for its round "enlightenment window" framing a garden view, and one of the region's best spots for hydrangeas in June.

For a longer visit, several hiking courses connect Kamakura's temples through the wooded hills — the Daibutsu Hiking Trail links the Great Buddha area to Kita-Kamakura in about an hour, passing smaller temples most day-trippers never see.

The seaside and Enoshima

Being a coastal town, Kamakura has beaches that are popular in summer and a generally breezy, relaxed atmosphere year-round. The charming Enoden railway trundles along the coast, connecting Kamakura with the nearby island of Enoshima — a scenic add-on with a shrine, gardens, an observation tower, and sea-cave walks. The Enoden ride itself, rattling between houses and along the shoreline, is a nostalgic pleasure — the stretch near Kamakurakoko-mae station, where the tracks run right alongside the beach with Enoshima in the distance, has become a pilgrimage site for fans of the anime Slam Dunk, whose opening scene was set there, and it's a genuinely pretty stop even without that context.

Where to eat

Kamakura's local specialty is shirasu (whitebait), served fresh over rice bowls (shirasu-don) at restaurants near the coast — a genuinely local dish you won't find as easily in Tokyo. Komachi-dori, the pedestrian shopping street running from Kamakura Station toward Tsurugaoka Hachimangu, is lined with snack stalls, croquette shops, and sweets, good for grazing between temples rather than a sit-down meal.

How to do it

Kamakura is easy and close — about an hour from Tokyo Station or Shinagawa via the JR Yokosuka Line direct to Kamakura Station, making it one of the simplest day trips. The main sights are reachable by local train (including the scenic Enoden) and some walking, and a relaxed half-day to full day covers the highlights. Its proximity and laid-back vibe make it ideal if you want temples plus a sea breeze without venturing far, or a gentler day than the mountain trips — and deciding which day trips to slot into a short Tokyo stay, and which to skip, is exactly the kind of call the complete Japan route guide helps make.

Practical tips

  • Start in the morning to enjoy the sights at a relaxed pace, especially in summer when the beaches and trains get busy.
  • Wear comfortable shoes — there's walking between sights, some of it uphill or along trails.
  • The Enoden line is scenic and fun; a day pass can be handy if you're hopping between coastal stops.
  • Combine the Great Buddha and Hase-dera, which are close together near Hase Station.
  • Carry small change for temple entry fees — most sites charge a modest fee (typically a few hundred yen) and don't always take cards.
  • Weekends and holidays get noticeably busier, especially around the Great Buddha and Komachi-dori — a weekday visit is meaningfully calmer if your schedule allows it.

Bottom line

For an easy, scenic day trip combining a magnificent open-air Buddha, historic temples, a nostalgic coastal railway, and sea air, Kamakura is hard to beat. Its proximity to Tokyo and relaxed charm make it a refreshing, low-stress escape from the city — the gentlest of the classic day trips, and a good pick if the rest of your itinerary has been packed with temple-hopping and you want a day that trades a little history for sea air.

title: Nara Day Trip Guide: Deer and a Giant Buddha
excerpt: Nara is the easiest, most charming day trip from Kyoto or Osaka — free-roaming deer, a giant bronze Buddha, and ancient temples. Here's how to visit.
content:
Nara is one of Japan's most delightful day trips — easy to reach from Kyoto or Osaka, compact, and home to a giant bronze Buddha plus a park full of famously friendly deer. As Japan's capital even before Kyoto (in the 8th century), it's rich in history, with several of the country's oldest and most important temples. It's a favorite of travelers of every age. Here's how to do it.

The deer of Nara Park

Nara's most beloved attraction is its free-roaming deer, which wander the large central park and are considered sacred messengers of the gods. You can buy special deer crackers (shika senbei) from vendors to feed them, and many of the deer have famously learned to bow in exchange for a treat. They're wild animals, so be gentle and follow the posted guidance — they can get pushy when they smell crackers — but interacting with them is a genuine highlight, especially for families and kids.

Todai-ji and the Great Buddha

Todai-ji is Nara's crowning sight — a vast wooden temple housing an enormous bronze Buddha (Daibutsu), one of the largest in Japan, seated over 15 meters tall. The main hall is itself one of the largest wooden buildings in the world, and the scale of both hall and statue is genuinely awe-inspiring. It's an easy, pleasant walk through the deer park to reach it, and it's the centerpiece of any Nara visit. Look for the "Buddha's nostril" pillar with a hole said to grant good fortune to those who can squeeze through.

More to see

  • Kasuga Taisha: a beautiful, atmospheric shrine famous for its hundreds of bronze and stone lanterns, set in the forest at the edge of the park.
  • Kofuku-ji: a historic temple near the park, one of Nara's most important. Note that its landmark five-story pagoda is currently undergoing major restoration and is covered by scaffolding (and not visible) until around 2034 — but the temple's National Treasure Museum and other halls remain well worth seeing.
  • Nara Park itself: lovely for a relaxed stroll, with grassy expanses, woodland, and ponds.
  • Naramachi: a preserved old merchant district of traditional machiya houses, now full of shops, cafes, and small museums.

Where to eat

Naramachi's cafes and small restaurants are the best bet for a sit-down meal — look for kakinoha-zushi (sushi wrapped in persimmon leaves), a Nara specialty that traveled well before refrigeration and is still a signature regional dish. Nara is also known for producing narazuke, vegetables pickled in sake lees with a distinctive sharp flavor — a good, portable souvenir if you want to bring a taste of the trip home.

How to do it

Nara is the easiest and closest of the Kansai day trips, reachable in well under an hour by train from Kyoto or Osaka — the JR Nara Line runs direct from Kyoto Station in about 45 minutes, and the Kintetsu Nara Line from Osaka's Namba Station in a similar window, with the Kintetsu-Nara Station actually closer to the park than the JR one. Slotting an easy day like this alongside a longer or more demanding one elsewhere is part of pacing a trip well, something the complete Japan route guide gets into. Most of the main sights are clustered around Nara Park within easy walking distance of one another, so it's a low-stress, mostly on-foot day. A half-day covers the highlights (deer, Todai-ji, a shrine or two); a full day lets you add Naramachi and explore at a relaxed pace.

Practical tips

  • Start in the morning to enjoy the park before it gets busy and the deer are most active.
  • Buy deer crackers from official vendors, and don't feed the deer other food; keep maps, tickets, and snacks tucked away, as the deer will nibble at bags and paper.
  • Be calm and gentle around the deer — bow back to them for a fun interaction, but supervise small children.
  • Wear comfortable shoes; it's a walkable but spread-out park with some gentle hills toward Kasuga Taisha.
  • Most sights are close together, so you'll need little transport once you arrive — though a bus helps reach the park from JR Nara Station, since it's a longer walk than from the Kintetsu station.
  • If you're coming from Kyoto and holding a JR Pass, the JR Nara Line makes sense even though it's the slightly longer walk; if you're not pass-holding or coming from Osaka, the Kintetsu line's proximity to the park often wins out.

Bottom line

For history, a giant Buddha, and the simple joy of bowing deer, Nara is an easy and rewarding day trip that almost every first-timer loves. If you have a spare day from Kyoto or Osaka, it's the one to choose — just plan around the pagoda being under wraps for now (scaffolding is expected to stay up until around 2034), and let the deer and the Daibutsu steal the show.

title: Nikko Day Trip Guide: Shrines in the Forest
excerpt: Nikko offers spectacular UNESCO shrines among cedar forests and mountain scenery, a rewarding day trip north of Tokyo. Here's how to visit.
content:
Nikko is a mountain town north of Tokyo, celebrated for its spectacular UNESCO World Heritage shrines and temples set among towering cedar forests, plus waterfalls and lake scenery in the highlands beyond. It's a rewarding day trip for travelers who love history and nature, and a striking change of scene from the capital. Here's how to approach it.

The shrines and temples

Nikko's centerpiece is its complex of ornate shrines and temples, the most famous being Toshogu Shrine, the lavishly decorated mausoleum of Tokugawa Ieyasu, founder of the shogunate that ruled Japan for centuries. Unlike the usual restraint of Japanese religious architecture, Toshogu is a riot of intricate carving, gold leaf, and color — including the famous carved panels of the "three wise monkeys" (see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil) and the sleeping cat. The complex sits among ancient, soaring cedars that give it a majestic, almost mystical atmosphere. Exploring the shrines is the heart of a Nikko visit. Look closely at the carvings and you'll notice recurring animal and floral motifs beyond the famous monkeys and cat — Toshogu carries over 5,000 carvings in total, and even a focused visit only takes in a fraction of the detail packed into the complex.

Nature beyond the shrines

With more time, the area around Nikko offers beautiful mountain scenery up in the Oku-Nikko highlands: the dramatic Kegon Falls, the serene Lake Chuzenji, and marshland and hiking in the national park. These take extra travel time (a winding mountain road) from the shrine area, so a full day or an overnight helps if you want both the shrines and the nature. In autumn, the foliage here is spectacular, typically peaking in mid-to-late October around Lake Chuzenji's higher elevation — three to four weeks ahead of Kyoto's famous autumn color in late November, which is worth knowing if your trip dates line up with one but not the other.

Getting there and eating

The most direct route is the Tobu Railway from Tokyo's Asakusa Station, with limited express trains reaching Tobu-Nikko Station in about two hours; a JR/Tobu through-service also runs from Shinjuku. Around the shrine area and Nikko's small town center, look for yuba (tofu skin), a local specialty served in everything from simple bowls to multi-course kaiseki-style meals — a distinctive dish worth trying here specifically, since it's more associated with Nikko and Kyoto than most other stops on a first trip.

How to do it

Nikko is reachable from Tokyo by train, taking a bit longer than closer day trips like Kamakura, so it makes for a fuller day out — worth weighing against your other day-trip options when you're deciding how to spend limited time near Tokyo, something the complete Japan route guide helps sequence. Many travelers focus on the shrine complex, which is walkable once you arrive (with some uphill), and add the highland nature only if time allows. Starting early maximizes what you can see and is essential if you want to combine shrines and waterfalls in one day.

Highlights checklist

  • Toshogu Shrine — the ornate, gold-adorned centerpiece, with the three wise monkeys and sleeping cat carvings.
  • Rinno-ji and Futarasan Shrine — the other major components of the UNESCO complex among the cedars.
  • Shinkyo Bridge — a picturesque vermilion bridge arching over the river near the entrance to the shrine area, and the traditional starting point of the shrine complex.
  • Kegon Falls and Lake Chuzenji (with extra time) — dramatic waterfall and lake scenery up in the highlands, reached by a winding mountain road with dozens of switchbacks known as Irohazaka.

Practical tips

  • Start early — the travel time means you'll want a full day to do it justice.
  • Consider a regional pass (such as the Nikko-area passes) for the train and local buses if you'll venture to the highlands.
  • Dress in layers; the mountains are cooler than Tokyo, and it can be snowy in winter, with the highland road sometimes closed in the coldest months.
  • Wear comfortable shoes for walking the forested, slightly hilly shrine grounds.
  • Guided tours are available if you prefer not to handle the logistics, and can be efficient given the distance.
  • Autumn weekends bring heavy traffic on the Irohazaka road up to the highlands — the 20-minute drive can stretch to 2-3 hours at peak foliage, so budget extra time or lean on the train/bus combination instead of a rental car.

Bottom line

Nikko rewards the longer journey with some of Japan's most spectacular shrine architecture in a stunning ancient-forest setting, plus highland waterfalls and lakes for those who venture further. For history and nature lovers willing to make a full day of it, it's one of the most memorable day trips from Tokyo — pair it with a plate of local yuba before you head back, and you'll have covered the town's two signature experiences in a single visit.

title: How to Plan Your First Japan Itinerary (Step by Step)
excerpt: Planning your first trip to Japan? Here's a step-by-step guide to building an itinerary that fits your time, avoids rookie mistakes, and flows.
content:
Planning a first trip to Japan can feel overwhelming — so much to see, an unfamiliar transit system, and a fear of getting it wrong. It's actually very manageable once you follow a logical order. Here's a step-by-step guide to building a first-timer itinerary that fits your time, dodges the common rookie mistakes, and flows smoothly.

Step 1: Decide your trip length and dates

Be realistic about time, including the long flight and jet lag. A week is the classic first-trip length; ten days is the sweet spot if you can swing it. Exactly which weeks to target — and which to avoid entirely — is its own decision with real stakes for pricing and crowds; see our full breakdown of the best (and worst) times to visit before you lock in dates.

Step 2: Choose your cities (and don't overdo it)

The single biggest rookie mistake is trying to see too much. For a first trip, Tokyo and Kyoto are the essential pair, linked by a 2h15m Shinkansen ride. Resist adding a string of far-flung cities; you'll spend the trip on trains and packing rather than actually experiencing any one place. Two bases for a week, three for ten days or more, is the sweet spot — the math is simple: every extra city costs you the better part of a travel day (packing, checking out, the ride itself, checking in again), so a week split across four cities means you've burned a quarter or more of your trip just moving.

Step 3: Add day trips instead of more hotels

Rather than relocating constantly, base in your cities and reach everything else on day trips: Hakone (Mt Fuji and onsen) and Nikko or Kamakura from Tokyo; Nara, Osaka, and Himeji from Kyoto. This is the secret to seeing a lot while unpacking little — you keep one hotel, one set of unpacked bags, and simply ride out and back. It also gives you a built-in escape valve: if a day trip destination turns out to be rainy or you're just tired, you can swap it for a slower day in your base city without unraveling any hotel bookings, which isn't true if that same stop were a scheduled relocation.

Step 4: Sketch the route geographically

Lay your trip out so it flows in one direction — typically east to west (Tokyo → Kyoto → maybe Osaka/Hiroshima) — rather than zigzagging. Within each city, group sights by area and tackle one zone per day. This minimizes wasted transit time more than any other single choice.

Step 5: Book flights open-jaw

Fly into Tokyo and out of Kansai (Osaka) — or vice versa — so you don't backtrack to where you started. Open-jaw tickets often cost little or no more than a round trip and can save you a whole travel day, since the alternative (flying round-trip out of Tokyo) means either ending your Kyoto time early to train back, or tacking on an extra return leg you didn't need. Price both ways before you book — occasionally a round trip really is cheaper, in which case eating one backtrack is worth the savings, but don't assume it without checking.

Step 6: Sort transport

Two decisions here, each with its own dedicated breakdown: get an IC card (Suica/Pasmo) on arrival for effortless local transit, and work out whether the Japan Rail Pass is actually worth it for your specific route — don't buy it by default, since its price increase means it no longer pays for itself on every itinerary.

Step 7: Book accommodation near stations

Choose central, well-connected neighborhoods near a train or subway station — in Japan's transit cities, that proximity beats almost any other amenity. Book early for peak seasons, and consider one special night in a ryokan or onsen inn.

Step 8: Reserve the time-sensitive things

A few experiences sell out and should be booked ahead: teamLab tickets, popular restaurants, any guided tours, and peak-season accommodation. Leave the rest flexible — over-planning every hour is its own rookie mistake.

Common first-timer mistakes to avoid

  • Too many cities — the number-one error; stay put more.
  • No jet-lag buffer — keep day one light.
  • Backtracking — fly open-jaw and route in one direction.
  • Buying the JR Pass reflexively — do the math first.
  • Over-scheduling — leave room to wander and rest.
  • Ignoring the holiday crunches — avoid Golden Week and the like.

Why this order matters more than any single step

Notice what happens across these eight steps: your dates (Step 1) determine how crowded and expensive your cities are, which affects how many bases actually make sense (Step 2), which determines whether the JR Pass math works out (Step 6), which changes your total budget enough to affect where you book (Step 7). Get one of these wrong in isolation and the fix is easy — get several wrong together, in the wrong order, and you end up back-solving a trip that's already booked, which is a much worse position. That's the real skill in planning Japan: not any single decision, but sequencing them so each one is made with the previous ones already settled. The complete Japan route guide is built around exactly that sequencing, worked out in full rather than step by step.

Bottom line

Building a first Japan itinerary is really just a sequence: pick your length and dates, choose Tokyo and Kyoto as bases, add day trips, route it west, fly open-jaw, sort transport, book near stations, and reserve the few things that sell out. Follow that order, keep the pace humane, and you'll have a first trip that's smooth, rich, and very likely the first of several.

title: Japan in 7 Days: The Perfect First-Timer Itinerary (Tokyo + Kyoto)
excerpt: A complete 7-day Japan itinerary for first-time American visitors — Tokyo, a day trip, the bullet train to Kyoto, and Nara. Day by day, with what to book.
content:
One week is the classic first trip to Japan, and the route nearly everyone converges on is Tokyo plus Kyoto, linked by the bullet train, with a day trip or two mixed in. It balances big-city energy, traditional culture, and an easy pace without backtracking. Here's a day-by-day plan built for first-time American visitors, traveling in spring or autumn at a moderate pace.

Before you go: the essentials

A few things make this itinerary run smoothly. As a US passport holder you enter visa-free for up to 90 days — no visa needed. Because you'll do the Tokyo–Kyoto round on the Shinkansen, price the Japan Rail Pass against individual tickets before you buy — for a simple two-city week with one round trip, the pass usually loses: a 7-day pass runs around ¥50,000, while a Tokyo–Kyoto round-trip ticket costs roughly ¥28,000, so you'd be paying nearly double for coverage you only partly use. Get a Suica or Pasmo IC card the moment you land for all local transit, and remember there's no tipping anywhere. Book timed-entry sights like teamLab ahead.

Days 1–3: Tokyo

Day 1 — Arrival and Shibuya/Shinjuku

Fly into Haneda or Narita and head to your hotel (Shinjuku, Shibuya, or Asakusa all make great bases). Take it easy on jet lag — get your IC card, then ease in with the Shibuya Crossing and a wander through Shibuya and Shinjuku, ending with dinner in an atmospheric alley like Omoide Yokocho.

Day 2 — Old Tokyo and the skyline

Start early at Senso-ji in Asakusa, the city's oldest temple, then explore the Akihabara electronics district and head up Tokyo Skytree for the view. Mix in the Tsukiji Outer Market for a seafood lunch if you have time.

Day 3 — A day trip or teamLab

Use day three for a day trip — Hakone for hot springs and Mt Fuji views, or Nikko for forest shrines — or stay in the city for the immersive teamLab digital art museum and Meiji Shrine beside Harajuku. Pick based on the weather: a clear forecast makes Hakone's Fuji views worth it.

Day 4: Shinkansen to Kyoto

Ride the Shinkansen from Tokyo to Kyoto — about 2 hours 15 to 2 hours 30 on the Hikari service, city center to city center, and a bucket-list experience in itself. Grab an ekiben (station bento) before boarding and enjoy it on the way; sit on the right-hand side of the train for a chance at spotting Mt Fuji as you pass. Drop your bags and spend the evening soaking up Gion, the historic geisha district, with dinner along the riverside Pontocho Alley.

Days 5–6: Kyoto

Day 5 — Eastern Kyoto

Explore the eastern hills: Fushimi Inari with its tunnels of red torii gates (go early to beat both the crowds and the heat), then up through the preserved Higashiyama streets to Kiyomizu-dera and its hillside veranda. This is Kyoto at its most atmospheric, and the walk between the two easily fills a full, unhurried day on its own.

Day 6 — West and north

Head to Arashiyama for the bamboo grove and riverside scenery in the morning, then over to Kinkaku-ji, the dazzling Golden Pavilion, in the afternoon. Group sights by area like this to minimize travel time across the city.

Day 7: Nara day trip and departure

On your last day, take the short train to Nara to see Todai-ji's giant bronze Buddha and the famous free-roaming deer in the park — a perfect, all-ages finale. Alternatively, tick off any final Kyoto sights you missed. Then depart from Kansai Airport (KIX), which is the natural exit point from the Kyoto/Osaka side — flying out of KIX instead of returning to Tokyo saves you a backtrack.

Ways to adjust

The spine above flexes easily. On day three choose Hakone, Nikko, or a city day depending on your interests and the weather. In Kyoto you can swap in Nijo Castle, the Imperial Palace, or the Philosopher's Path. If you have more time, add Osaka for food or Himeji for its spectacular castle. The structure — Tokyo first, bullet train to Kyoto, day trips around the edges — is what makes a first week in Japan flow, and it's the same underlying logic that the complete Japan route guide extends to longer trips with more cities in play.

What to book ahead

For a smooth trip, sort these early, especially if your dates fall in a peak travel window, when both flights and hotels fill up and prices climb well ahead of the actual dates: your flights (search flexible dates and consider flying into Tokyo, out of Kansai, to avoid backtracking), your hotels in Tokyo and Kyoto, and any experiences or tours with limited capacity like teamLab or guided day trips. Locking these in ahead of time is the difference between a relaxed week and a scramble to find a room or a ticket at the last minute.

title: 1 Week in Japan: The Perfect First-Timer Itinerary
excerpt: Seven days is enough for a superb first trip. Here's a day-by-day 1-week Japan itinerary covering Tokyo, Kyoto, and easy day trips.
content:
One week is the classic length for a first trip to Japan, and it's enough to see the essentials without rushing — if, and only if, you keep the route simple. The proven approach is to base in just two cities, Tokyo and Kyoto, linked by the Shinkansen, with day trips on either side. Here's a balanced, realistic day-by-day plan — not an idealized one that assumes zero fatigue or perfectly timed trains.

The shape of the week

Resist the urge to cram in five cities. Two well-chosen bases — Tokyo then Kyoto — let you settle in, unpack once per city, and use the trains for day trips rather than constantly relocating. The bullet train between them takes about 2 hours 15 minutes, so the one big move mid-trip is painless.

Days 1–3: Tokyo

Day 1 — arrival and the west side. Land, get an IC card and mobile data at the airport, and head to your hotel. Ease into the day with Shibuya Crossing, Harajuku, and the calm of Meiji Shrine, then a relaxed dinner — don't overschedule while jet-lagged. If your flight lands early enough, this is also a reasonable day to drop bags and walk rather than nap, which helps reset your body clock faster.

Day 2 — old Tokyo. Start early at Senso-ji in Asakusa, head to Tokyo Skytree for the view, then Akihabara for the electronics-and-anime spectacle. An evening in an izakaya, ideally one of the small counter spots rather than a chain, for a more local feel.

Day 3 — your pick. Either the immersive teamLab digital art museum plus upscale Ginza, or a day trip to Hakone for hot springs and Mt Fuji views. teamLab is the better rainy-day choice; Hakone needs a clear-ish forecast to be worth the trip out.

Day 4: Travel to Kyoto + Nara or Fushimi Inari

Take a morning Shinkansen to Kyoto (about 2h15m). After dropping your bags, ease in with an afternoon at Fushimi Inari, walking up through its tunnels of red torii gates, or head straight out to Nara for the giant Buddha and friendly deer if you arrive early enough — Nara works best as a full morning-to-afternoon outing rather than a rushed afternoon add-on, so only choose it here if your Shinkansen was an early one.

Days 5–6: Kyoto

Day 5 — eastern Kyoto. The Higashiyama district: wander the preserved streets up to Kiyomizu-dera, then explore Gion, the geisha quarter, ending with dinner along Pontocho Alley. Going early is more important here than almost anywhere else on the trip — Sannenzaka and Ninenzaka are genuinely a different, much calmer place before 9am.

Day 6 — west and north. The Arashiyama bamboo grove early, then the golden Kinkaku-ji, and if you have energy, the Zen rock garden at Ryoan-ji. These three sights sit far enough apart that a taxi or bus between them, rather than walking the whole loop, keeps the day from turning into a transit slog.

Day 7: Day trip or slow finish

Use your last full day for a day trip to Nara (if you didn't on day 4) or Osaka for food and energy — or slow down, revisit a favorite spot, and shop for souvenirs. Then it's time to head home, ideally flying out of Kansai (KIX) to avoid backtracking to Tokyo. If you do add Osaka, Dotonbori's food scene alone can fill the whole day, and it's a genuinely different register from either Tokyo or Kyoto — louder, brasher, and focused almost entirely on eating well.

Tips to make it flow

  • Fly open-jaw — into Tokyo, out of Osaka/Kansai — to save a backtrack.
  • Start early at the famous sights to beat crowds, and group each day by area.
  • Build a light first day to shake off jet lag.
  • Sort your IC card at the airport, and check whether a rail pass actually pays off for this specific route before buying one — it often doesn't anymore for a route this simple.

If a week feels tight

The week above already assumes a fairly brisk pace, slotted efficiently with minimal slack. If reading through it left you feeling like something has to give, that's a real signal, not a personal failing: a week genuinely is tight for Tokyo plus Kyoto plus day trips, and deciding what to trim (skip a day trip? cut a Tokyo neighborhood? shorten Kyoto?) without wrecking the flow is a harder call than it looks on paper. The complete Japan route guide works through exactly that kind of trade-off in more depth than a single sample itinerary can.

Bottom line

A week built around Tokyo and Kyoto, with Hakone, Nara, or Osaka as day trips, covers the best of Japan for a first-timer without feeling rushed. Keep the route simple, lean on the trains, and you'll come home already planning your return.

title: 10 Days in Japan: The Ideal Itinerary
excerpt: Ten days is arguably the sweet spot for Japan. Here's a day-by-day itinerary adding Osaka, Hakone, and Nara to the Tokyo–Kyoto core.
content:
Ten days is arguably the sweet spot for a first trip to Japan, and the length most returning travelers wish they'd booked the first time — enough to see the two great cities properly, add the best day trips, and work in Osaka, all without feeling rushed. Here's a balanced day-by-day itinerary that covers the country's essentials at a comfortable pace.

The shape of the trip

The plan above uses three bases — Tokyo, then the Kansai region (Kyoto or Osaka), with day trips throughout. The extra days over a one-week trip let you slow down, add Hakone and Nara, and experience Osaka's food scene. Fly open-jaw (into Tokyo, out of Kansai) to avoid backtracking.

Days 1–4: Tokyo

Day 1 — arrival. IC card, data, hotel, and an easy first afternoon (Shibuya, Harajuku, Meiji Shrine). With ten days to work with, there's no need to fight jet lag on day one — a slow arrival pays for itself later.

Day 2 — old Tokyo. Senso-ji, Tokyo Skytree, Akihabara, an izakaya night.

Day 3 — modern Tokyo. teamLab digital art, Ginza, and a neighborhood you're drawn to (Shinjuku's nightlife, Ueno's parks, or Odaiba's bayfront) — this is the day to follow a personal interest rather than a checklist, since the itinerary has slack to absorb it.

Day 4 — day trip to Hakone. Hot springs, the scenic mountain loop, and Mt Fuji views on a clear day. Consider an overnight in a ryokan here if you'd like to add an onsen-inn experience — with ten days total, giving up a Tokyo day for a Hakone overnight is an easier trade than it would be on a shorter trip.

Day 5: Travel to Kyoto

Morning Shinkansen to Kyoto (about 2h15m). Ease in with Fushimi Inari's torii gates in the afternoon, or settle in and explore the downtown and Nishiki Market — with ten days, there's no pressure to pack the arrival afternoon full, so let energy levels decide.

Days 6–7: Kyoto

Day 6 — eastern Kyoto. Higashiyama's old streets, Kiyomizu-dera, Gion, and Pontocho for dinner.

Day 7 — west and north. Arashiyama's bamboo grove and Tenryu-ji, then Kinkaku-ji and Ryoan-ji.

Day 8: Nara day trip

An easy trip from Kyoto to Nara — the giant bronze Buddha at Todai-ji and the famous free-roaming deer in Nara Park. Half a day covers the highlights, leaving the afternoon to relax or explore more of Kyoto, browse Nishiki Market, or simply rest — by day 8 a genuine slow afternoon is worth more than another sight.

Days 9–10: Osaka

Day 9. Move to (or day-trip into) Osaka — Osaka Castle by day, then the neon and street food of Dotonbori by night: takoyaki, okonomiyaki, kushikatsu. Osaka's food culture is dense enough that a single night of grazing between stalls can stand in for a sit-down dinner entirely, and most visitors prefer it that way.

Day 10 — departure. A final morning of food or last-minute shopping, then fly out of Kansai (KIX), conveniently close to Osaka and Kyoto. Build in more transit buffer than feels necessary — a missed international flight is a much bigger problem than an hour spent waiting at the gate.

Tips

  • Fly open-jaw into Tokyo and out of Kansai.
  • On the JR Pass: with this much travel, price a 7-day pass against your actual Shinkansen and JR fares — but note a single Tokyo–Kyoto hop plus local Kansai trips often still comes out cheaper on individual tickets. Do the math, and consider a regional Kansai pass for the Osaka/Kyoto/Nara leg.
  • You could base entirely in Kyoto or Osaka for the Kansai portion and day-trip between them, since they're only ~15 minutes apart by fast train.
  • Work in one ryokan/onsen night (Hakone or a Kansai option) for a traditional experience.
  • Leave at least one afternoon genuinely unplanned — with ten days you can afford it, and it's usually where the trip's best unplanned moment happens.

Why ten days is the sweet spot

The extra three days over a one-week trip don't just add more sights — they add slack, and slack is what actually makes a Japan trip feel good rather than just efficient. A week-long itinerary has almost no room for a bad-weather day, a place you fall in love with and want more time in, or simple fatigue; ten days absorbs all three without falling apart. Getting that balance right — enough structure to not waste time, enough slack to not feel like a schedule — is a harder design problem than it looks, and it's exactly what the complete Japan route guide is built around.

Bottom line

Ten days lets you experience Tokyo and Kyoto in depth, add Hakone and Nara as day trips, and enjoy Osaka's food scene — the fullest version of the classic first trip. It's relaxed, varied, and comprehensive without overreaching, and for many travelers it's the ideal length.

title: 2 Weeks in Japan: A Comprehensive Itinerary
excerpt: Two weeks lets you go beyond the basics. Here's a 14-day Japan itinerary adding Hiroshima, Miyajima, and more to the classic route.
content:
Two weeks in Japan is a luxury that lets you go well beyond the classic Tokyo–Kyoto core — adding Hiroshima and Miyajima, more day trips, an onsen town, and time to slow down and wander. Here's a comprehensive 14-day itinerary that still keeps a sane pace.

The shape of the trip

Fourteen days supports three or four bases moving roughly west across the country: Tokyo, the Kansai region (Kyoto/Osaka), and Hiroshima, plus day trips and an onsen night woven in along the way. Fly open-jaw if you can — into Tokyo, out of Osaka or Fukuoka — so your route is a steady progression west rather than a there-and-back trip that revisits Tokyo at the very end. The Shinkansen makes the whole west-to-east spread easy and comfortable, turning what would be a genuinely long haul by car into a series of relaxed two-to-three-hour hops.

Days 1–4: Tokyo and Hakone

Three days in Tokyo covers the icons (Senso-ji and old Asakusa, the Shibuya Crossing, teamLab, Tokyo Skytree), plus time to wander a neighborhood or two at a slower pace. Add a Hakone day trip or overnight for hot springs and Mt Fuji views on the scenic loop of mountain railway, ropeway, and lake cruise. See our 7-day itinerary for a fuller day-by-day breakdown of this stretch.

Days 5–6: Around Tokyo

With extra time, add another day trip — Nikko for spectacular UNESCO forest shrines, or Kamakura for the seaside Great Buddha — and a slower day to explore a Tokyo neighborhood in real depth or revisit a favorite from earlier in the stay. This is where a two-week trip starts to feel meaningfully different from a rushed first week: you have room to double back to what you loved.

Day 7: Travel to Kyoto

Ride the Shinkansen to Kyoto. Spend the afternoon easing in — Fushimi Inari's torii tunnels if you want an early highlight, or a gentler wander through downtown and Nishiki Market if you'd rather start slow.

Days 8–10: Kyoto and Nara

Two full days in Kyoto, grouped by area to minimize crosstown travel: eastern Higashiyama and Gion one day, western Arashiyama and Kinkaku-ji the next. Add a day trip to Nara for Todai-ji's giant Buddha and the park's free-roaming deer. Add an evening tea experience or a quieter temple like Ryoan-ji's rock garden if you have appetite for more.

Day 11: Osaka

A day (or overnight) in Osaka — Osaka Castle by day and a night of street food in neon-lit Dotonbori. It's an easy, quick hop from Kyoto, close enough that some travelers even day-trip it without changing hotels.

Days 12–13: Hiroshima and Miyajima

Shinkansen west to Hiroshima. Spend a day at the deeply moving Peace Memorial Park and Museum, and a day on nearby Miyajima island to see the famous torii gate (check the tide table — it only "floats" at high tide), hike or ride the ropeway up Mt Misen, and meet yet more friendly deer roaming the island.

Day 14: Departure

Travel back toward your departure airport, or fly out of Kansai if your routing allows it, with a final morning free for anything you missed. If you based cleverly and flew open-jaw, you've looped steadily west across the country without ever doubling back far — exactly the kind of routing choice the complete Japan route guide walks through for trips with this many moving pieces.

Alternative add-ons

With two weeks, you can swap in other regions depending on your interests:

  • Koyasan — a sacred mountain with temple-lodging (shukubo) and morning prayers, near Osaka.
  • Takayama and the Japan Alps — traditional towns and mountain scenery.
  • Kanazawa — a refined city with one of Japan's finest gardens.
  • An onsen town like Kinosaki for a relaxing night or two.

Tips

  • This is the itinerary where a JR Pass is worth pricing carefully — a 14-day pass runs around ¥80,000, while individual tickets for Tokyo–Kyoto–Hiroshima and back add up to roughly ¥45,000–70,000 depending on exactly how many legs you ride, so the two options often land close together rather than one clearly beating the other. The single biggest lever is whether you fly open-jaw (into Tokyo, out of Kansai): skipping the return leg back to Tokyo removes a big chunk of point-to-point cost and usually tips the math against the pass. Price both for your exact route before deciding.
  • Build in slower days — two weeks is long enough that constant sightseeing burns out; leave room to wander.
  • Use luggage forwarding (takkyubin) between cities so you're not hauling bags on every train.
  • Add at least one ryokan/onsen night for a traditional experience.

Bottom line

Two weeks lets you experience Japan comprehensively — the two great cities, the best day trips, Osaka's food, and the meaningful detour to Hiroshima and Miyajima — at a pace that still leaves room to breathe. It's the trip that turns a first-timer into a lifelong returnee.

title: 3 Weeks in Japan: The Extended Itinerary
excerpt: Three weeks in Japan opens up the whole country. Here's how to extend beyond the classics to Kanazawa, the Alps, Koyasan, and further afield.
content:
Three weeks in Japan is a rare gift — enough to cover the classic highlights and venture well off the standard trail into mountain towns, sacred sites, and regions most first-timers never reach at all. Here's how to think about an extended trip without it becoming an exhausting, sprawling checklist that leaves you as tired as you were before you left.

The strategy for a long trip

With 21 days, the temptation is to add destinations endlessly, turning the itinerary into a checklist that spans the entire country — resist it. The better approach is to do the classic route at a relaxed pace, then add a few deeper regions with real time in each, plus genuine rest days built in rather than treated as wasted time. Quality of experience beats quantity of cities almost every time on a trip this long; three unhurried regions beat eight rushed ones. Use the Shinkansen and luggage forwarding to move efficiently between a handful of well-chosen bases, and resist the pull to add "just one more stop" once your route is already set.

Week 1: Tokyo and the east

Four to five days in Tokyo with day trips (Hakone for Mt Fuji and onsen, plus Nikko or Kamakura), exploring the city's neighborhoods in real depth rather than rushing the icons — a full afternoon in Shimokitazawa or Yanaka, say, rather than a photo stop. Time to enjoy the food scene properly, from depachika basement food halls to a proper izakaya crawl, at a slower pace than a short trip ever allows.

Week 2: Central Japan and Kansai

Head into central Japan on the way west: the traditional Edo-period streets of Takayama and the thatched-roof villages of the Japan Alps, and the refined gardens and culture of Kanazawa, home to Kenroku-en, one of Japan's three great gardens. Then settle into Kyoto for several unhurried days (temples, Gion, Arashiyama), with day trips to Nara and Osaka — with this much time, you can actually let a rainy afternoon become a museum day instead of a crisis.

Week 3: West and beyond

Continue west to Hiroshima and Miyajima (the Peace Park and the torii gate that floats at high tide). With remaining time, choose a deeper detour based on your interests:

  • Koyasan — temple lodging (shukubo), morning meditation, and the vast, moss-covered Okunoin cemetery on a sacred mountain.
  • The Kii Peninsula — ancient Kumano Kodo pilgrimage trails and remote onsen villages, genuinely far from the usual tourist track.
  • Kyushu — the southern island, with the hot-spring capital of Beppu, active volcanoes, and Fukuoka's renowned food scene.
  • Hokkaido — the northern island, for national-park wilderness, seafood and dairy, and (in winter) some of the best powder skiing on earth around Niseko.
  • The Japan Sea coast or Tohoku — rural, scenic, and barely touristed by international visitors even in peak season.

Build in rest

Three weeks of nonstop sightseeing will wear anyone down, no matter how much you love Japan. Deliberately schedule slower days: a second day in a place you love, an onsen-town stay where you do nothing but soak and eat kaiseki, or an unstructured day to wander a neighborhood with no itinerary at all. These often become the most memorable parts of a long trip, precisely because nothing about them was planned.

Tips

  • The JR Pass is most likely worth it on a trip like this — a 21-day nationwide pass runs around ¥100,000, and with this much long-distance travel across Tokyo, central Japan, Kansai, and Hiroshima (plus whatever western detour you add), the fares for equivalent point-to-point tickets can genuinely exceed that. Still price it against your specific planned Shinkansen fares before buying, since the answer always depends on your exact route — that pricing decision is exactly the kind of thing the complete Japan route guide is built to walk through in detail.
  • Luggage forwarding (takkyubin) between bases is invaluable over three weeks — send bags ahead a day and travel light on transit days instead of hauling everything through train stations.
  • Don't change hotels more than necessary; use day trips from a few well-placed bases rather than a new hotel every two nights.
  • Mix the famous and the obscure — the contrast between a crowded icon and a quiet backstreet is part of what keeps a long trip feeling fresh rather than repetitive.
  • Vary your accommodation: city hotels, a ryokan, a temple stay, an onsen inn — each is a genuinely different experience, not just a place to sleep.

Bottom line

Three weeks lets you go beyond the postcard Japan into its mountains, sacred sites, and quieter regions — but the secret is restraint: cover the classics well, add a few deep detours, and build in rest. Done right, an extended trip reveals a richer, more varied Japan than most visitors ever see.

title: 5 Days in Japan: A Short-Trip Itinerary
excerpt: Only have five days in Japan? Here's how to make the most of a short trip — focused on Tokyo and Kyoto, with no wasted time.
content:
Five days in Japan is short, but it's absolutely worthwhile — the key is to keep it tight and not try to see everything. With careful focus on Tokyo and Kyoto, you can still experience the country's two essential faces — modern neon energy and centuries-old tradition — without either one feeling rushed. Here's how to make every single day count, hour by hour if needed.

The strategy for a short trip

With only five days, don't spread yourself thin. Stick to two cities — Tokyo and Kyoto — connected by one Shinkansen ride, and accept that you'll skip some things (that's what a return trip is for). Prioritize the absolute highlights and group each day by area to avoid wasting time in transit — every hour spent crossing town to catch "one more thing" is an hour not spent actually experiencing wherever you already are, and on a trip this short that trade-off compounds fast.

Days 1–2: Tokyo

Day 1. Arrive, sort an IC card and data, drop bags. Spend the afternoon on the west side — Shibuya Crossing, Harajuku, and Meiji Shrine — keeping it light if you're jet-lagged. On a five-day trip you genuinely can't afford to lose day 2 to exhaustion, so err on the side of an early dinner and bed over squeezing in one more sight.

Day 2. Old Tokyo: Senso-ji in Asakusa, Tokyo Skytree for the view, and either Akihabara or teamLab depending on your interests. Cap it with an izakaya dinner. Skip Ginza and the further-out neighborhoods this trip — they're real Tokyo, but a five-day itinerary doesn't have room for a third Tokyo day.

Day 3: Travel to Kyoto + Fushimi Inari

Morning Shinkansen to Kyoto (about 2h15m). Drop your bags and head to Fushimi Inari in the afternoon to walk through the iconic red torii gate tunnels — magical in the late-afternoon light as crowds thin. You don't need to walk the entire mountain trail to the summit; the first 20-30 minutes through the densest cluster of torii gates covers the part almost everyone comes for, and turning back there rather than pushing on saves real energy for the days ahead.

Days 4–5: Kyoto

Day 4. Eastern Kyoto: the Higashiyama streets up to Kiyomizu-dera, then Gion at dusk with dinner on Pontocho Alley.

Day 5. Arashiyama's bamboo grove early, then Kinkaku-ji, before heading to the airport — ideally flying out of Kansai (KIX) to avoid returning to Tokyo. Build real buffer into this day: an afternoon flight gives you breathing room if the morning runs long, while an evening flight risks a stressful dash to the airport with your bags in tow.

What you're (deliberately) skipping

Five days means leaving out day trips like Hakone and Nara, plus Osaka — and that's fine. Trying to add them would turn a relaxed short trip into an exhausting dash. Save them for next time; almost everyone who visits Japan comes back. You're also skipping most of the "second-tier" Tokyo and Kyoto neighborhoods — Shinjuku's nightlife, Kyoto's Nishiki Market, a proper temple crawl beyond the two or three biggest names — which is a genuinely different experience from a 10-day trip, not just a shorter version of one.

Tips

  • Fly open-jaw (into Tokyo, out of Kansai) — essential on a short trip to avoid a wasted backtrack.
  • Skip the JR Pass — for a single Tokyo–Kyoto round trip (really a one-way here), individual tickets are cheaper.
  • Pack light so the one city change is quick and painless — a carry-on-only approach genuinely changes how manageable train travel feels.
  • Book any must-do timed experiences (like teamLab) in advance, since you have no slack to reschedule.
  • Confirm your Kyoto hotel is walkable to a train or bus stop — on a trip this compressed, you can't afford long transfers eating into your two Kyoto days.

Is five days actually enough?

Honestly: it's enough to fall in love with Japan, not enough to see it properly. The itinerary above works because it's ruthless about scope — two cities, no day trips, no detours — and that ruthlessness is the whole trick. If you find yourself wanting to add "just one more stop" while reading this, that instinct is exactly what turns a smooth five-day trip into a rushed one; deciding what a short trip can and can't hold is a big part of what the complete Japan route guide helps with, whether this is your only trip or the first of several.

Bottom line

Five days is enough for a genuine taste of Japan if you stay focused on Tokyo and Kyoto and don't overreach. You'll see the neon and the temples, ride the bullet train, and eat brilliantly — a short but complete first impression that leaves you wanting more — and for a lot of travelers, that's the whole point of a five-day trip in the first place.

title: Asakusa & Old Tokyo Area Guide
excerpt: Asakusa is Tokyo's most traditional district, home to Senso-ji temple and old-town charm. Here is what to see, eat, and why it is worth basing here.
content:
Asakusa is where Tokyo holds onto its past — a district of temples, traditional shops, and old-town atmosphere on the city's northeast side. It's the best place to feel historic Tokyo, and a favorite base for travelers who prefer charm and value over glitz. Here's what to do.

Senso-ji

The centerpiece is Senso-ji, Tokyo's oldest temple, founded in the year 645 according to temple tradition and rebuilt after WWII bombing destroyed the original structure. You enter through the iconic Kaminarimon ("Thunder Gate") with its giant red lantern, then walk the Nakamise shopping street — nearly 90 stalls lined up over roughly 250 meters, selling traditional snacks and souvenirs — up to the grand temple hall and its five-story pagoda. Go early in the morning, ideally before 8am, to experience it before the tour groups arrive; the temple grounds themselves never close, so an early or after-dark visit shows a genuinely different, much quieter side of the same place.

Around the temple

  • Nakamise Street: great for street snacks — try ningyo-yaki (small cakes shaped like temple landmarks) or freshly cooked senbei rice crackers — and traditional souvenirs like folding fans and yukata.
  • Backstreets: wander beyond the main drag, particularly Denboin-dori, for craft shops, old-style eateries, and a noticeably quieter feel than the crowded temple approach.
  • Sumida River: nearby for riverside walks and boat cruises — a water bus runs from Asakusa down to Odaiba, a scenic and relaxed way to see a different stretch of Tokyo.
  • Rickshaw rides: a fun, if touristy and pricier, way to tour the old streets with a guide who narrates as you go.
  • Kimono rental: popular here for strolling the traditional setting in style — same-day rental-and-return shops cluster around the temple approach, no reservation always required though booking ahead guarantees your size and style.

Tokyo Skytree nearby

Just across the river from Asakusa rises Tokyo Skytree, at 634 meters one of the world's tallest towers, with two observation decks, extensive shopping at its base (Tokyo Solamachi), and an aquarium. It's an easy add-on to an Asakusa visit and offers sweeping views, especially near sunset when the city lights start coming on. On the way, look for the Asahi Beer Hall's gold "Flamme d'Or" sculpture across the river — an odd, unmissable piece of Tokyo architecture locals have nicknamed after its resemblance to a certain bodily object, and a fun photo stop either way.

Why stay here

Asakusa is a popular base for first-timers who want traditional atmosphere and often better value than the western hubs — it's genuinely worth comparing hotel prices here against Shinjuku or Shibuya for the same trip dates. (This article contains affiliate links — if you book through them we earn a small commission at no extra cost to you.) The trade-off is that it sits on the eastern side, so reaching Shibuya/Shinjuku takes a bit longer — typically 25-35 minutes by subway — but it's still an easy train ride, and waking up near Senso-ji, with the morning quiet before the crowds, has its own magic that the western hubs can't offer.

Practical tips

  • Visit Senso-ji early or in the evening (the lit-up temple at night is beautiful and uncrowded).
  • Combine Asakusa and Skytree into one easy half-day, crossing via the Azumabashi bridge.
  • The area is walkable and well connected by subway (Ginza and Asakusa lines) and the Tsukuba Express.
  • Carry cash for the small traditional shops along Nakamise and the backstreets — many don't take cards.

Where to eat

Beyond Nakamise's grab-and-go snacks, Asakusa has some of Tokyo's most respected old-school restaurants for tempura and unagi (grilled eel), several running for generations out of the same modest storefronts — a contrast to the flashier dining scenes in Shibuya or Ginza. The backstreets west of the temple (Hoppy Street, named for a beer substitute popular with an older postwar generation) are lined with casual, cash-only izakaya serving grilled skewers and cheap drinks — an atmospheric, unpretentious place for an evening that feels a world away from Shinjuku's neon version of a night out.

A neighborhood that survived

Much of what makes Asakusa feel different from the rest of Tokyo is simply that it's older: the area was the city's main entertainment and theater district for centuries before Shinjuku and Shibuya existed in any recognizable form, and while the 1923 earthquake and WWII bombing destroyed most of the original buildings (Senso-ji included), the street layout and small-shop character were rebuilt close to how they'd always been, rather than redeveloped into the high-rise districts that now define central Tokyo.

Bottom line

For old-Tokyo atmosphere — temples, traditional shops, and a slower pace — Asakusa is unmatched in the city. Pair it with the modern spectacle of Skytree next door, and you've got one of Tokyo's most rewarding and characterful areas.

title: Shibuya & Harajuku Area Guide
excerpt: Youthful, fashionable, and endlessly walkable — here is what to do in Tokyo's Shibuya and Harajuku districts, from the famous crossing to Meiji Shrine.
content:
Shibuya and Harajuku sit side by side on Tokyo's west side and together form the city's youthful, fashion-forward heart. They're easy to combine into a single day of wandering, and the contrast between the two — electric energy giving way to boutique calm giving way to a forest shrine — is one of the best single-day snapshots of what makes Tokyo interesting. Here's what to see in each.

Shibuya

Shibuya is anchored by the world-famous Shibuya Crossing, the scramble intersection where up to 3,000 people surge across in every direction at once when the lights change. Walk it once at street level, then watch the spectacle from above — the Shibuya Sky observation deck and the window seats at the Starbucks overlooking the crossing are both popular vantage points, though Sky charges admission and the Starbucks is first-come, first-served. Nearby is the Hachiko statue, a beloved meeting spot named for a dog famous for waiting at the station daily for its owner even after his death — it's tiny in person and often mobbed, but worth the two minutes.

What to do in Shibuya

  • Experience the crossing from street level and from above.
  • Shop the youth-fashion department stores like Shibuya 109, the district's iconic multi-floor fashion mall.
  • Explore the side streets around Center Gai and Miyashita Park for cafes, restaurants, and bars.
  • Take in a city view from Shibuya Sky or one of the newer rooftop observation decks.

Harajuku

A short walk or one train stop from Shibuya, Harajuku is the center of Tokyo's youth and street fashion. Takeshita Street is its famously colorful, crowded pedestrian lane packed with quirky shops, crepe stands, and whatever trend is peaking that season — it's genuinely narrow, so expect shoulder-to-shoulder crowds on weekends. Just beyond, Omotesando offers a completely different register: a wide, tree-lined boulevard of designer boutiques and architecture from name-brand international architects, more Champs-Élysées than teen fashion strip — flagship stores from Prada, Dior, and a rotating cast of Japanese and international designers occupy buildings by well-known architects, and even if shopping isn't the point, the street itself is worth a slow walk for the architecture alone. The side alley of Ura-Harajuku (behind the main street) is where independent boutiques and vintage shops cluster, a better bet than Takeshita Street itself if crowds aren't your thing.

Meiji Shrine

The contrast that makes this area special: right beside busy Harajuku lies Meiji Shrine, set in a tranquil forest of some 120,000 trees donated from across Japan when it was built. The wooded approach and grand torii gates create one of the most peaceful spots in central Tokyo — a perfect counterpoint to the surrounding bustle. Don't skip it. Adjacent Yoyogi Park is worth a wander too, especially on a weekend when street performers, musicians, and picnicking locals turn it into one of the best people-watching spots in the city.

How to combine them

A natural plan: start with the calm of Meiji Shrine and Yoyogi Park in the morning before the crowds build, wander Harajuku (Takeshita Street and Omotesando), then end in Shibuya for the crossing and an evening out — dinner in the side streets, then the crossing again after dark, when the neon signage makes it a genuinely different sight than the daytime version. It's an easy, walkable progression from serene to electric, and showcases Tokyo's range in a single day. The whole loop is also a reasonable base for your stay: Shibuya in particular is well-connected and worth checking for a hotel if you want nightlife and transit links over old-Tokyo atmosphere. (This article contains affiliate links — if you book through them we earn a small commission at no extra cost to you.)

Practical tips

  • Weekends are extremely crowded in Harajuku and at the crossing — go early or on a weekday if you can, especially for photos.
  • It's all walkable, but the JR Yamanote line connects the stations if you tire.
  • Great area for people-watching and street food (just don't eat while walking) — Takeshita Street's rainbow cotton candy and crepe stands are the classic photo-ops.
  • Meiji Shrine is free to enter, though the inner garden carries a small fee.

Where to eat

Shibuya's side streets hide far better food than the main crossing area suggests — Nonbei Yokocho ("Drunkard's Alley"), a tiny cluster of postwar-era bars and yakitori counters tucked under the train tracks near Shibuya Station, is worth seeking out for something more local than the chain restaurants facing the crossing. Harajuku leans casual and photogenic: beyond the Takeshita Street crepe stands, the side streets around Cat Street (between Harajuku and Omotesando) have a good concentration of cafes if you want to sit down rather than eat on the move — remember, eating while walking is generally frowned on in Japan, so a bench in Yoyogi Park or a cafe seat is the better call than strolling with a crepe in hand.

title: Shinjuku Area Guide: What to Do in Tokyo's Busiest Hub
excerpt: Shinjuku packs nightlife, shopping, parks, and the world's busiest station into one district. Here is how to make sense of it, plus where to eat and where to stay.
content:
Shinjuku is Tokyo at its most concentrated — a district that crams together neon nightlife, vast shopping, skyscrapers, and a beautiful park, all around one of the world's busiest train stations. It can be dizzying, so here's how to navigate it and what not to miss.

Unlike Asakusa's old-Tokyo character or Shibuya's youth-fashion pull, Shinjuku doesn't have a single identity — it's several districts stacked on top of each other, split cleanly by the station itself. That split is the easiest way to hold the area in your head: government towers and hotels to the west, department stores and daytime shopping to the east, and the nightlife strip of Kabukicho and Golden Gai just beyond that.

The station (don't panic)

Shinjuku Station is enormous and famously confusing — over 200 exits across a sprawling underground maze that connects JR lines, Tokyo Metro, and several private railways. The trick: know which exit you need before you arrive (follow signs to landmarks or compass directions — East Exit for Kabukicho and the department stores, South Exit for the bus terminal and newer developments, West Exit for the skyscraper district), and don't be afraid to just surface and reorient if you get turned around underground. Once outside, the district itself is entirely walkable and far less intimidating than the station beneath it.

What to do

  • Shinjuku Gyoen: one of Tokyo's loveliest parks, a genuinely serene escape with French, English, and Japanese formal gardens — gorgeous in cherry blossom season (late March–early April) and worth the small entry fee any time of year. Arrive early on weekends to beat the crowds.
  • Omoide Yokocho ("Memory Lane"): atmospheric lantern-lit alleys of tiny eateries and bars, most seating just a handful of people at a time — perfect for an early evening of yakitori and a beer before the crowds peak.
  • Golden Gai: a warren of minuscule themed bars, a Tokyo nightlife institution — many welcome visitors, some don't, and cover charges are common; a little research on a specific bar before you go smooths the experience.
  • Kabukicho: the big, brash entertainment district next to Golden Gai — vibrant and intense at night, with the giant illuminated Godzilla head over the Toho building as its unofficial mascot.
  • Skyscraper district & observation decks: the west side's cluster of towers includes free city views from government building observatories — a real money-saver next to paid options elsewhere in Tokyo.
  • Shopping: huge department stores (Isetan is the standout for its basement food hall alone), electronics megastores, and endless retail radiating out from every station exit.

Where it fits in your trip

Shinjuku is a top choice for where to book a hotel thanks to its transport links and all-in-one convenience — nearly every train line in Tokyo touches it, which matters more than almost anything else when you're basing a short trip in one spot. (This article contains affiliate links — if you book through them we earn a small commission at no extra cost to you.) It's also a top choice to go out at night. By day it's strong for shopping and the park; by night it's the heart of Tokyo nightlife. Many travelers pass through its station constantly regardless of where they stay, simply because so many connections run through it.

Eating in Shinjuku

Beyond Omoide Yokocho's yakitori stalls, Shinjuku rewards a little food planning: the basement food halls (depachika) under Isetan and the other department stores sell restaurant-quality bento and desserts for a fraction of a sit-down meal, ideal for a park picnic at Gyoen. Ramen options cluster around the East Exit, and Golden Gai's bars often serve a simple food menu alongside drinks if you want to combine the two. For a sit-down meal with a view, several of the skyscraper hotels on the west side have restaurant floors open to non-guests — a good option if you want Shinjuku's energy from a quieter vantage point.

Getting to and from Shinjuku

Shinjuku sits on the JR Yamanote loop line, so it connects directly to Tokyo Station, Shibuya, Ueno, and most of the city's other major hubs without a transfer — one of the reasons it works so well as a base. It's also the departure point for several long-distance highway buses, and the Narita Express runs directly here from Narita Airport (about 80 minutes), making Shinjuku one of the more convenient bases if you're flying into Narita rather than Haneda.

Practical tips

  • Use station lockers or your hotel to avoid hauling shopping around all day — Shinjuku's stores are numerous enough that bag fatigue sets in fast.
  • Trains stop running around midnight — plan your night accordingly, or budget for a taxi back if you're out late in Kabukicho or Golden Gai.
  • In Kabukicho at night, ignore touts offering to lead you to a bar or club — stick to venues you researched or found yourself.
  • The west side is skyscrapers and calm; the east side is shopping and nightlife — a useful mental map when you're deciding which direction to walk out of the station.

Bottom line

Shinjuku rewards a bit of fearlessness — embrace the energy, pick a couple of targets (the park by day, the alleys by night), and don't let the giant station intimidate you. It's Tokyo's beating heart and an essential part of the city, whether you base yourself here or just pass through.

title: Where to Stay in Tokyo: Best Neighborhoods for First-Timers
excerpt: Shinjuku, Asakusa, or Shibuya? Here's how Tokyo's best base neighborhoods compare for first-time American visitors, and who each one suits.
content:
Tokyo is genuinely enormous, so where you base yourself shapes your whole trip — how much time you spend on trains each day, what's genuinely walkable at night, and the vibe you wake up to every single morning. The good news: the city's train network is genuinely so good that almost any central neighborhood works well. For a first visit, three areas stand out clearly, with a fourth worth considering if you want something a little more refined and quiet.

How to think about location

The single most useful thing to know is the JR Yamanote line — a loop that circles central Tokyo and stops at most of the neighborhoods you'll want. Staying on or near the Yamanote loop, or on a Tokyo Metro subway line, means you can reach almost anything quickly. With a Suica or Pasmo IC card in hand, getting around the whole system becomes effortless within a day or two. So "best neighborhood" is really less about raw centrality and more about which atmosphere actually fits you and how you like to travel.

Shinjuku — best all-rounder

If you want one base that does everything, Shinjuku is the safe pick. It's a major transit hub, so trains radiate everywhere, and it packs in dining, shopping, nightlife, and green space (Shinjuku Gyoen, one of the city's loveliest parks) within walking distance. It's busy and bright — the neon-and-crowds Tokyo people picture — with the atmospheric little lantern-lit alleys of Omoide Yokocho for evening food.
